stem: Define heredity. Explain the mechanism of hereditary changes.
solution: Heredity: Heredity is the transmission of characters (traits) from parents to their offspring through genes, generation after generation. Mechanism of hereditary changes: A gene is a specific segment of DNA that controls a particular character. During reproduction, genes are passed from parents to offspring. Hereditary changes (variations) arise mainly in two ways — (a) Mutation: a sudden change in the sequence or position of the nucleotides of a gene alters the character it controls; and (b) Recombination: the reshuffling and new combinations of parental genes during meiosis and sexual reproduction. Such changes, if they occur in the gametes, are inherited by the next generation and, over long periods, accumulate to bring about evolution. Thus genes carry heredity, and changes in genes are the basis of hereditary variation.

chapter: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part 1
stem: Write any four stages of mitosis and explain any two of them.
solution: The four stages (of karyokinesis) in mitosis are: (1) Prophase, (2) Metaphase, (3) Anaphase, (4) Telophase. Explanation of any two: (a) Prophase — the chromatin condenses into distinct chromosomes, each seen as two sister chromatids joined at the centromere; the nuclear membrane and nucleolus gradually disappear and the spindle fibres begin to form. (b) Metaphase — the chromosomes arrange themselves in a single row at the equatorial plane (equator) of the cell and the spindle fibres get attached to the centromere of each chromosome. (Anaphase — the centromeres split and the sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles; Telophase — the chromosomes reach the poles, uncoil, and two new nuclear membranes form giving two daughter nuclei.)

chapter: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part 2
stem: Explain with examples types of asexual reproduction in unicellular organism.
solution: Types of asexual reproduction in unicellular organisms: (1) Binary fission — the parent cell divides into two equal daughter cells, e.g. Amoeba, Paramoecium, bacteria. (2) Multiple fission — the nucleus divides repeatedly and the cell splits into many daughter cells at once, e.g. Plasmodium (malarial parasite). (3) Budding — a small outgrowth (bud) develops on the parent, grows and separates to form a new individual, e.g. yeast. (4) Spore formation — special reproductive cells (spores) are produced which germinate into new individuals, e.g. some algae and fungi. In all these, a single parent produces genetically identical offspring without the fusion of gametes.

stem: Which fuel is used in thermal power plant? Write any two problems associated with this type of power generation.
solution: Fuel used in a thermal power plant: coal (fossil fuel); some plants also use oil or natural gas. Two problems associated with thermal power generation: (1) Burning of coal releases large amounts of \(CO_2\), oxides of sulphur and nitrogen, smoke and ash, causing air pollution, global warming and acid rain. (2) Coal is a non-renewable (exhaustible) fossil fuel whose reserves are limited and getting depleted, and disposal of the huge quantity of ash produced is also a problem.

Three characteristics of phylum Mollusca: (1) The body is soft and unsegmented, and is usually protected by a hard calcareous shell. (2) A muscular foot is present which is used for locomotion (and in some for capturing food). (3) A soft skin fold called the mantle covers the visceral mass and secretes the shell; the body shows bilateral symmetry and organ-system level of organisation. Examples: snail (Pila), mussel, octopus.

stem: What are the constituents of acid rain? What are its two effects on earth's surface?
solution: Constituents of acid rain: acid rain mainly contains sulphuric acid \((H_2SO_4)\) and nitric acid \((HNO_3)\). These are formed when oxides of sulphur \((SO_2)\) and oxides of nitrogen \((NO_x)\) — released by burning of fossil fuels — dissolve in rain water. Two effects on earth's surface: (1) It makes the soil and water bodies (lakes, rivers) acidic, which harms crops, plants, aquatic animals and reduces soil fertility. (2) It corrodes and damages buildings, bridges, metal structures and marble monuments (e.g. the Taj Mahal).

stem: Write down the reasons, effects and remedial measures taken for any one disaster seen or heard by you.
solution: Disaster: Flood. Reasons: heavy and continuous rainfall, overflowing of rivers, breaching or failure of dams, blocked or poor drainage, and deforestation which reduces the soil's capacity to hold water. Effects: loss of human and animal life; damage to houses, roads, railways, crops and property; contamination of drinking water leading to epidemics of waterborne diseases; and disruption of electricity, transport and communication. Remedial measures: timely warning and evacuation of people to safe places; setting up relief camps providing food, clean water and medicines; construction of embankments/dams and proper drainage systems; afforestation to control run-off; and rehabilitation and financial help to the affected people. (Any one disaster — flood, earthquake, cyclone, landslide — with its reasons, effects and remedies is acceptable.)
